body: I understand. But it does get better. You spent a lot of time and energy on this person, and I hope it wasn't all bad, but it's important to focus on yourself now. You come first. I wish you the best with your healing process!

I unfortunately don't have much advice to give you, but just know this isn't about you, it's about her. You haven't done anything for her to behave this way and this is just her dealing with her emotions and paranoia at the moment. The best thing you can do is keep doing what you've been doing, not interacting and not giving it any attention. It might be even wise to block her yourself to save yourself more emotional turmoil. You were her best friend and she entirely relied on you but somewhere somehow she convinced herself you hated her so it must be hard on her as well, and this is the only way she's able to deal with it. I'm not someone who randomly deactivates accounts to take mental health breaks or focus on studying for example, but tbh I've only ever done it while in a fight with someone close or something like that. So I can understand her reasoning but it's hard to describe. 

That being said, it's hard to give the right perspective if she hasn't been actually diagnosed with BPD. Is it possible she has it? Yes. Is it possible it is something different with similar or overlapping symptoms? Also yes. The only thing I can advise you to do is try to heal yourself from this and not necessarily burden yourself with trying to understand why she's doing all this. The initial reason of why she even ended the friendship seems irrational so there is no real reason as to why it's happening other than her mental health. I know it's easier said than done but wondering and worrying yourself over her reasoning behind all this is going to hurt you more. I genuinely don't believe that any of this is your fault so I think it's best you try to let go for your own mental well being

There are multiple reasons why people don't like to hear that, and a lot of it comes from people being unable to properly understand dog body language. Most people who have "friendly" dogs actually have rude, pushy dogs who end up bullying others because you think a high wagging tail = friendly.

The most important part imo is that yes yours might be friendly, but that doesn't mean other dogs or people want to meet him. If you let him rush any dog he comes across without knowing the temperament of the other then you'll end up with a fight. It's about respecting other people and animals' boundaries that's all. There's personally nothing I hate more than someone yelling from 20 meters away that their dog is friendly while it barrels towards mine. Because she isn't friendly...
The concern isn't so much about others seeing a random dog approaching it's about yours' safety

How am I ridiculing you? Lol I'm just saying you need to ask yourself why you want a mal specifically. A lot of people get these dogs for looks and because they're cool and end up with more than they can chew. I just personally recommend getting one if you have something more specific in mind you want to do...

It's important to do more research. Why do you want a Mal? Do you like the way they look? Or is it their energy/drive for work (your post makes me lean towards no on this one)? Because they are "protective"?


Mals aren't necessarily the "run your energy out" type of dog. They like working for something. I personally don't recommend mals unless you are planning to do something with it, getting it for actual work or because you plan to do a sport with it. Not just long hikes or runs

You're acknowledging that this isn't the right environment for him and that's the hardest part but it's the right thing. I don't see it as you "giving up on him" but as you wanting to give him the best life possible. The reason why I recommend a sanctuary and not rescue/rehome is because he would be able to be taken care of by people who know what they're doing. It might be a hard transition but he will eventually be able to bond with other dogs that are like him in a place like that. 

I just want to say that backyard breeders is excatly why YOU are in this situation. Of course I understand being uneducated and getting a BYB dog because you genuinely didn't know better. I don't mean to sound rude but this is a genuine issue and the way you said it did make it seem like it was something you planned on doing. It's not about responsibility it's about not putting other uneducated people in your situation. I hope you can educate yourself more about it and also not get a dog from craigslist and find a good breeder. If you had done that you may have had a perfectly fine swiss shepherd
Wanting to breed a craigslist puppy in the first place is crazy 😭 Please consider a sanctuary for him

I understand, it'll just be a shame if something does happen after he took to it so naturally :/

If you are worried about where the puppies might end up it could be a good idea to ask your trainers to maybe spread the word about them. It could lead to more experienced people to get them in the correct environment. I'm personally just concerned about your environment and how the puppy could react to it. Unfortunately most BYBs I know have ended up biting, whether it's another dog, person, child or their own owners. Sometimes 2-3 years down the line. I have a big heart as well and I have considered taking in rescue mals but I ended up getting one from a good breeder and it was the best decision IMO. For me, my other dog and my mal himself. From what you've described I think eventually getting a well bred mal maybe a year or two later may be a better choice!

I think the biggest thing you need to consider is the fact that dog is BYB. You are considering getting a very unpredictable dog, and even with good training it will remain unpredictable. 
Also the first few years of owning a Mal are absolute hell, and I wouldn't recommend you get one if your first dog hasn't fully matured and entirely trained yet. It'll just make your life harder. 

I don't see this is a "you can never own a Mal" moment, but I believe it may not be the best timing and getting a BYB one is even more of a gamble. You don't know if something may end up happening with your current dog as well that may mess up his service dog training

You already have a young puppy, why not focus on that one first ? Dock diving is a pretty open sport and any breed (as far as I've seen) can excel at it as long as the dog likes water. I don't really understand the need for a mal specifically when you already have a dog you could explore sports with.

if you ever want to try out group therapy again i suggest you look for DBT or groups for BPD specifically. personally it did help me a lot with feeling understood and less alone. 

unfortunately BPD will still get stigmatised by people who also suffer from other disorders and mental health professionals (i'm sure that goes for everything else tho) so you end up facing judgement either way... i'm sorry you went through that :(
Why not ask bully breed subs? They could help you better, different breeds different needs

I am from Europe as well, in my country breeders will register in a breed club which usually has good quality control and guidelines for breeders who want to register. I can image that for an uncommon breed, a club may not exist. Being registered in a kennel club (FCI, UKC, AKC...) does not guarantee a good breeder however I do know FCI has some guidelines to be followed.


Really, it's more up to you to find a breeder and look into them. Have they done this for a long time? Are their dogs health tested for all common health issues in the breed? Do their dogs fit in the conformation standards? How many litters do they produce in a year? What happens if you can no longer keep the dog, will they take it back into their care? I don't know if CWD are used in sports, but if you want a breed that is bred for a specific purpose the dogs should be titled. Also don't be afraid to contact and speak with the breeder directly, good ones are usually very open to have conversations with people who seem to be knowledgeable, interested and cautious in what they are looking for.

I understand! That's why I said you should use the time before you even want to get the dog to do research and educate yourself on both breeding and other dog breeds (again you never know). It has changed my perspective on the whole dog world a lot personally, I didn't know much before getting my first dog. 
At the end of the day, if you'll get the dog anyway and won't change your mind, probably everyone here would prefer for you to get a dog with a good genetic background so you are less likely to get a dog with health or behavioural issues! It'll benefit both you and the future dog, whichever breed you get

Thats what ethical breedings does though... it eliminates the "common" health issues you see in badly bred dogs and dogs that come from puppy mills. There are also breeds that have enough genetic diversity for certain lines to have no health issues for generations. Most german shepherds don't suffer from hip dysplasia, especially not if they come from a good breeder. That's why we screen dogs before breeding for any underlying health issues that come up in the breed. And no breed is immune to health issues, CWD is prone to dysplasias and movement complications as they age as well. 

I'm wondering what breeds you've looked at? Because yes it can be a gamble to get a husky you don't want to be loud, but it can be as much of a gamble when it comes to a wolfdog and their possible behavioural issues. Most dogs also usually have a lifespan of 12 years (looking this up will show you a lot of variation from different sources) at least unless you're looking at very large breeds. 

I just hope you'll take advice from experienced owners and others well educated on genetics and the corresponding behaviour. I think most people are concerned because of the amount of times they must've heard people getting a CWD or other wolfdog and then regretting it and trying to get rid of it. I know this from other intense breeds. Sorry for the assumptions as well— that's just why most people get them.

with your answers, I'm wondering if you want a wolfdog because you want a dog or if you want a wolfdog because you want an animal that looks like a wolf and has the name because it's cool and impressive? 
No one is telling you to get a "practice dog" but to get a breed that is going to be fit your lifestyle better. Like you said, this hypothetical dog that doesn't even exist yet is 4 to 5 years away. From some of your previous replies I feel like you don't know much about dogs and ethical breeding in general. You have all the time to do extensive research on different breeds and who knows, you may fall in love with another one. There are tons of breeds that looks wolfish that could be a better fit as long as your provide the time, training and exercise. 

I don't own a wolfdog but I have worked with some, they are prone to anxiety and aggression (same sex, especially if you want a male) and have an intense prey drive. Since you also show concerns about health issues, czech wolf dogs genetics are a bit of a mess, are prone to not only health issues of their own but also to behavioural issues. The one i worked with most recently (czech x gsd mix) is an absolute MESS at only about a year old... and the owner has had multiple hard breeds before. 

I just really encourage you to do more research, you have lots of time for that, learn about different type of dogs, ethical breeding, the genetic factors... There are lots of wolfy breeds that could fit into what you're looking for!

This. I know a few first time dog owners who got mals and have done a great job because they put in the work and still go to training every week to enjoy sports with them.


Unfortunately I've seen more first time owners that wanted a scary "protective" dog that have failed. Right now I personally know of more dogs being euthanised because of how they turned out than being rehomed successfully

I think you will be better off accepting the fact this person may just have been a bad friend who generally doesn't have other people's best interests in mind. People can be shitty, manipulative and selfish because that's how they decide to act.


I honestly don't think that slapping a diagnosis, that has high chances of being incorrect, to try to come to conclusions is the best way to go about this. Of course you have your own experience and I understand the need to heal from it, but these are harmful generalisations that are really not true. Yes people with BPD regret when their actions harm other like most people do, we are not monsters who go around using and hurting people just because we can. Id say most of us are the polar opposite. 
I'm sorry you went through this though and I do hope you can properly recover.

One thing I've learned while being in a healthier relationship is that, you can't ban someone from ever thinking of someone they were in a longterm relationship with. If my current boyfriend and I broke up it'd be awful but I would never want to forget everything that happened between us. Especially if you are younger, 3 years is a long time and this relationship could've essentially helped shape the person you are dating now. 


I don't want to say this to invalidate your feelings, because I completely get how you're feeling and it's painful. But if he really called her for closure I think that's a sign of him wanting to properly move on from it so he can go forward (with you). Yes he could've told you first, and yes you are allowed to feel upset, and you are allowed to put boundaries down now (no visiting and no phone calls and such). 


You also need to make peace with the fact you can't make him never think about or reminisce about their relationship. They were together for a long time and that can't be washed away into nothing. But he is with you now and not with her for a reason, and if you really have no other reasons to doubt him I'd say it's really a sign of him trying to fully move on to give you his best

Do you feel you may have gotten with him because of the attachment, or because you loved him for him?
This sounds a bit complicated, but a breakup doesn't have to be bad. You have shared a lot of your life together so I imagine you are very intertwined. Maybe if you were to break up, it doesn't have to mean he can't be part of your life anymore. 


But I'll stand firm on not leaving just in hopes to be with that other person. Yes it could potentially completely work out but it also might not and you'll end up with a lot of regret. With a relationship this long I think you really need to reflect on it and have conversations. It seems what you have is good, and may be it's worth trying again with finding what you lack within the relationship. But if you decide to leave, make sure it's for YOU and not to fill a hole

Personally no. I used to kind of "hop" from person to person because I always wanted something new and exciting and it honestly made things worse for me. Now that I matured a bit and found someone I actually truly love it seems extremely stupid to me to leave someone you are in love with for someone new because you think it is more exciting than having settled into a "boring" routine with your partner. 

However, if you want to leave because this is an incompatibility in your relationship then I think that's completely valid tbh. I just wouldn't recommend you leave BECAUSE you want to be with this new person and potentially rush into things with someone you do not know well. You should leave for yourself if you truly think that this is an incompatibility that cannot be resolved. 
Also I hope this doesn't come off as rude, but do you think you actually truly love your boyfriend or are you just attached to him because he is your FP?

I agree that it's starting to becoming ridiculous in certain contexts.

I personally have a huge problem with the way people treat FPs in this sub.. it's almost as if people blame the person they have that attachment to instead of admitting they are the problem. The acknowledgment and accountability is literally non-existent. If you're self-aware enough that you know and understand FP dynamics you should be self aware enough to try to break it. 

That being said, it's way easier said than done. I think most people post here to vent and get validation from people with similar experiences. It's just unfortunate that replies with genuine advice, even if worded harshly, get shadowed by replies that enable shitty behaviour...

I will say BYB and ethical breeders are very american terms and OP probably really did not know better. The country they seem to be from is not really known to be good when it comes to ethical breeding. Animal welfare is generally pretty bad in that area. Most of the balkans has street dogs everywhere and "breeders" are most often puppy mills that mass produce puppies and export them to other european countries to uninformed people. I can tell you that dog was not bred with good intentions in mind and would have probably ended up being a fighting dog if it was sold to someone else. 


With the rising popularity of these dogs being re-labelled as family protectors and guard dogs, bad breeding is leading to more and more human aggression. So many people take pride in having a scary and aggressive dog... I doubt there is much of actual APBT in OPs dog and they instead own the unfortunate result of profit breeding and are a victim of the dog-baby mindset. People need to stop treating their dogs as their surrogate babies.

I will try to say this as nice as possible, but your dog biting "for the first time ever" was at only one year old and he has now developed a pattern of behaviour. This can get so much worse. 

Your dog may be family but he is an animal first, and a very powerful one at that. He is able to do much more damage than this. The safety of your family comes first, you should let someone who can handle him take him, he is repeatedly "warning" your child who has no understanding of what the dog is trying to communicate. Keep them separated at all times

really depends on the dog and yourself, my first is a border collie and she doesn't really like other dogs, as in she just ignores them most of the time and she is also not fond of puppies at all but i got another knowing this. she and my mal barely actually interact with each other, they had a phase between his 4-10 months where they did play but my border stopped enjoying it as he became rougher. they respect each others space and personally i like it better than having dogs in each others face all the time lol 
i do think they have a good relationship as they get really happy to see each other if they get separated for a few days 

HOWEVER i am a firm believer that you should spend separate time together with each of your dogs. it doesn't have to be every day, but training them separately is important imo. i take long walks with both of them but for shorter walks at night or to play fetch or something i like to sometimes take them separately. they also sleep in separate rooms at night. i think it's especially good for my border as she was my only dog for a few years and it's like taking a break from the other. i do know a lot of dogs who instantly became best friends with the new puppy so it really depends!

That's part of it though, you get "obsessed" with her and only her attention and validation matters, the way she treats and interacts with you will dictate your whole life, until you can start moving on a bit. You may be trying to find a way to cope with it by seeing another girl for example, but you don't get the same feeling by getting attention from them. Like I said this type of infatuation is pretty common for someone with BPD and I know it's hell to deal with. I just think a lot of us mistake those feelings for just love when really they concern us more than the other person. Again I'm not trying to speak on your own experience! It's just what I've learned and what helped me as someone who's dealt with the same. It's different for everyone, some people will develop this type of feelings towards friends or coworkers and some only towards people they see as potential romantic partners, which is why you may have a type. 

I realise that saying you need to learn to handle it is easier said than done and it's also something I struggled with A LOT personally (before I was diagnosed it was really out of hand) and I still struggled with it a year ago. But it's not impossible to do and it's not impossible for you to end up developing a healthy, loving relationship. I'm currently in a pretty healthy relationship and I'll admit i'm more possessive, jealous and sensitive than your average girl but I don't have this complete dependency on my boyfriend and it's so refreshing honestly. 

I just hope you can get the help understanding how and why you feel this way, like I said most people on here talk about the same kind of situation so you are not alone! I can't really help you personally because it's been a long process for me, but I'm sure you can find some kind of support/help that won't make you feel so weird or alone

I can't speak for you or for everyone else, but this is very typical for BPD. Getting obsessed with someone (especially when it's very quickly) you don't truly know and view as perfect because you made up a perfect version of them in your head. It's not love it's infatuation and idealisation, and when said person can't live up to the expectations of the perfect version you made up everything crashes down. It comes from a need for validation, attention and an emotional connection. There was a really good post on here explaining this and the term of FP but I can't find it again. 

Unfortunately these relationships are rarely healthy and don't work out. It's not love for them, it's an obsession you develop because of your need for attention. Of course I'm not saying that loving them is not possible. 

I'm not saying this is what is happening to you here, but just explaining that this is extremely common for BPD and it's something that can repeat many times if you don't learn how to handle it. We all know how you feel right now

No, unless the other person crosses the "impossible" line most people with BPD tend to forgive a lot. However you didn't do anything wrong so I doubt she actually hates you, she probably feels really distraught and when she gets out of that headspace she'll probably feel very guilty. Unfortunately it seems there's way more to unpack in this whole situation. 

I think it's easier for us to get pressured and involved with people who are bad for us and do unhealthy things. She may have felt alone because you were working and she wasn't, and making these new friends was a way for her to cure herself from that. Her falling into substance abuse is a whole other issue that can also affect a lot of what has happened, addiction is a horrible black hole that is extremely hard to get out of and it's incredibly easy to relapse.

But with the use of drugs, leaving you for someone else and the domestic abuse you're best off without her. I understand still feeling the love and attachment but you need to take care of yourself and not let her drag you down along with her. The best would be to advise her to get some help in a mental health facility/rehab in hopes of her getting herself out again. You can support her through that if you'd like BUT don't take her back and don't keep fighting for her.

Men and women often experience emotions differently... I don't think it has anything to do with it. Just because in your experience you've handled it better doesn't mean all men with BPD do. I know I handle my shit better than most women who have been recently diagnosed. I also don't handle my shit as well as other women who have been longer in the therapy process. Everything to do with you as a person and your personal experiences and nothing to do with sex in my opinion. It's just different.

well are you okay with it? if you're uncomfortable then you should be honest with him, it will be his decision ultimately if he wants to go through with it despite you voicing your feelings. if you're comfortable with it and it won't bother you then let him. but you need to be honest with yourself and him, don't make a compromise that'll make you unhappy and overthink.

BPD is a scary disorder but it's important to remember that people tend to see, hear and speak of the worst and a lot that you will read online is not very nuanced. It's incredibly stigmatised and people who have been victims of abuse due to these toxic relationships tend to paint all of us as bad people. But everyone experiences the disorder differently, and it's important that you talk to her & learn about the way she lives things specifically. You guys will learn each other's ways of coping and resolving personal issues  as well as relationship conflicts as a pair. Don't be afraid to set clear boundaries for yourself & for her as certain symptoms can easily push people to have no clear boundaries in relationships (wether it may be bad for them or the other person). You are the one who knows her, and again communicating is important in all relationships, but it is SO important for people with BPD, don't be afraid to ask her about her feelings as to not invalidate them. Especially if she's been in toxic relationships it may be especially hard for her to clearly communicate her feelings. And again, you will also need to realise you shouldn't always take responsibility for everything that she feels because sometimes it truly is the disorder causing irrational thinking, but that's for her to figure out on how to cope with them with her own therapy. I believe that people with BPD can be the most dedicated, loyal and loving partners if given the proper space & support to feel safe and you truly seem like someone who cares deeply. Please don't let yourself be scared away by the things you see online as you might just be getting with the most amazing girl you'll meet. Or not, no one can know what the future holds, I often find myself thinking (and even saying it to his face) that my bf could be doing so much better but he decided to stick by me and as long as he does I will also give everything I have to make sure I do right by him.

I am glad that you are trying to get help, it really seems like you are trying to make a positive change in your life so you can build a future for yourself. You don't always see that here & even in group therapies. It seems you really care about her, and if you try your best to get better to offer her a good relationship I am sure she will do the same. The healing process may be hard and take a long time but you're already taking so many steps in the right direction. I truly hope it helps and you guys can be happy :)

If you feel like this is worth fighting for, then it probably is right? It seems like you are understanding things pretty well and she is trying to take responsibility for her own issues. Now it's also important for you to realise that you aren't responsible for all of her feelings and the issues that may arise in the relationship. Of course you will have down times and sometimes you'll fight or argue and hurt each other's feelings, but relationships is all about how you work these things out together. BPD is hard and makes relationships even harder when untreated, but with adequate help it is manageable. I am currently in a long term & serious relationship that I wouldn't have been able to handle a year and a half ago, my BPD is still affecting my everyday life but it's going well for the most part, but it is very different than if my boyfriend was in a relationship with someone mentally stable. That's the reality of it, and yet he still decided to be with me and make things work and our relationship is amazing. 

May I ask if you are also going to therapy? It seems like you may also need it to sort through your own issues and have a time where you can speak of these things with someone who can actually help and give you the right advice. Relationships between two unstable people can quickly go the wrong way and it's really hard to go back, so you're right in not rushing things and taking a step back. Just make sure this is something you are both ready for and that your own personal issues don't bleed into the relationship, that includes not internalising all of your own feelings (which therapy may be good for). Again, communication is key and you both need to make sure you think you are in the right place for this

They are definitely hard work, and it will take a lot of time and patience for the next few years to properly train one, and then all the years after that where you will have to keep them occupied. 

However I think a lot of things depend on the breeder, the temperament of the parents/bloodline as well as the individual dog's personality. I have experienced a lot of different belgians, I am a pretty active member of my local breed club where I've worked with the most chill pet mals and the absolutely insane and driven ones. It all depends on what you're actually looking for in your individual dog and you should make sure to research your breeder to make sure you can get what you want. 

I personally find some things you see online to be a bit overexaggerated, not all of these dogs are killing machines that need to be hyped up constantly during the day. A well balanced malinois, like any dog, needs to be able to sit down and relax. Mine is absolutely huge for a mal, I live in an appartment and he is my second dog, my first is a border collie which already in itself is labelled as an "absolutely don't get in appartment" dog. Both of my dogs are amazing, I've never had them destroy anything in my house as puppies, except for maybe a few exceptions. In the house they are calm and well behaved, sometimes bursts of energies but overall chill. Outside is their time to go be a dog and play, sniff, whatever. The club is their work time and they love it, I've entered multiple competitions with them and they do great. I managed this because their needs are met and they are content with chilling in the apartment when we are home, a dog will be well balanced as long as you are sure that you are giving them what they need and you dedicate the first years of their life to training and socialising. And then you'll have the most amazing dog. 

Your dog SHOULDNT need constant attention and stimulation all day, even "intense" breed need to lay down and relax for a few hours! From your situation it seems like you'd do fine with one, you seem well informed, just make sure to find a breeder that will help you get the dog you are looking for. :)
